source_spans.locator: Nature Reviews Neuroscience 15, published p.745, Abstract and opening discussion: spatial/temporal regularities, conditional probabilities and recent history provide information about likely forthcoming visual input

Nature Reviews Neuroscience 15, published pp.745-746, Decision-theoretic approaches / equations (1)-(2): current likelihood evidence is combined with prior probability; asymmetric priors shift the category decision criterion and bias choices

Nature Reviews Neuroscience 15, published pp.746-747, Sequential sampling / equations (3)-(5) and Figure 2: prior probability can enter as an early evidence offset or accumulation starting point; gain/drift is a distinct possible locus and simple origin bias fits key error patterns better

Nature Reviews Neuroscience 15, published pp.747-748, Figure 3 and 'Expectation biases pre-stimulus signals': stimulus probability modulates pre-stimulus decision-related activity and stimulus-selective sensory activity

Nature Reviews Neuroscience 15, published p.748, 'Neural signatures of expectation': reviewed evidence that prior-related effects can also alter evidence gain, particularly when current sensory evidence is weak or ambiguous; expected and unexpected evoked responses can differ

Nature Reviews Neuroscience 15, published pp.750-751, probability-versus-task-relevance discussion: event probability and current-goal relevance are conceptually separable, often experimentally entangled, and may affect sensitivity through distinct mechanisms

Nature Reviews Neuroscience 15, published pp.752-753, biological-implementation discussion and Conclusions: multiple computational descriptions can overlap; cellular mechanisms, top-down/bottom-up segregation, and origins of predictive neural signals remain unresolved

conditions: visual detection, recognition, or classification occurs when the probability of upcoming alternatives is asymmetric or otherwise informed by contextual, transition, frequency, or recent-history regularities
current sensory evidence has finite strength or precision and may be integrated over time
probability of occurrence must be distinguished from current-goal relevance because the reviewed literature often manipulates both with similar cueing paradigms
population: humans and non-human primates across the reviewed psychophysical, imaging, and single-neuron studies
substrate: reviewed decision-related parietal, frontal, motor, and oculomotor populations
task: detect, recognize, classify, or choose between visual alternatives under manipulated or learned differences in occurrence probability
temporal_scope: regularity-derived or experimentally supplied probability information can be available before the current stimulus
pre-stimulus neural activity can be biased before current sensory evidence arrives
after stimulus onset, sensory evidence is accumulated or otherwise combined with the prior-dependent state; prior influence is often strongest early or when evidence is weak

probability distribution over candidate visual alternatives before the current sensory evidence is fully incorporated

boundary separating alternative category responses in the signal-detection formulation
initial offset of a sequential evidence-accumulation process toward the more probable alternative

behavioral detection, recognition, classification, or alternative choice produced under asymmetric occurrence probabilities
baseline or build-up neural activity before stimulus onset in populations associated with the more probable response alternative
pre-stimulus activity in stimulus-selective visual populations corresponding to a more probable upcoming visual input
experimental change in occurrence probability or conditional probability through block frequency, predictive cues, or transition structure
reviewed psychophysical, electrophysiological, magnetoencephalographic, and functional-imaging measurements used to compare behavioral and neural states under different occurrence probabilities
whether a visual event or feature is relevant to the observer's current task or goal, treated separately from its occurrence probability

relations.description: environmental or learned regularities provide information from which a probability distribution over forthcoming visual alternatives can be formed
in the formal normative account, prior odds and current likelihood evidence jointly determine posterior support for the alternatives
asymmetric prior probability shifts the category criterion so responses are biased toward the more probable alternative
in a sequential-sampling implementation, asymmetric prior probability can produce an early offset in accumulated evidence toward the more probable alternative
behavioral choice reflects current sensory evidence together with prior-probability information rather than current evidence alone
reviewed studies report probability-dependent baseline or pre-stimulus changes in decision-related neural activity
reviewed studies report probability-dependent pre-stimulus activity in sensory populations associated with the more probable upcoming input
some reviewed accounts and data permit probability-dependent changes in evidence gain, with stronger effects when current sensory evidence is weak or ambiguous
experimental manipulations of occurrence or conditional probability alter the prior-probability state used in the reviewed comparisons

simple linear accumulation accounts distinguish an additive prior-dependent starting offset from multiplicative evidence gain, while the review notes that more complex nonlinear models can blur this separation
